To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) models trained for full-automation are not necessarily optimal under triage, (b) triage policies are deterministic threshold rules on the model-human error difference and (c) our gradient-based algorithm is guaranteed to find an optimal model-triage pair of increasing performance.

(a) predictive models may benefit significantly from algorithmic triages, (b) triage decisions should be made by thresholding the model error difference on a per-instance basis, and (c) gradient descent can find optimal models and triage rules.
(a) algorithmic triage can improve model performance, and (b) a gradient-based algorithm can efficiently find the optimal triage policies and predictive models for a given level of triage.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to best learn a model that is used under triage and provides the first formal analysis, algorithmic approach, and empirical evidence for this question.
the question of when a predictive model may be improved by triage.
the question of whether a predictive model should be fully automated, or whether it should be triaged to human experts.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the proposed method can provide better results than the state-of-the-art methods for the problem of learning under triage.
we introduce a gradient-based algorithm for differentiable learning under triage and show that it outperforms a number of baselines in a variety of tasks and data sets.
we have developed a framework for algorithmic triage that is theoretically grounded and empirically validated.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we introduce a novel learning framework, called differentiable learning under triage, and show that it can improve performance on a variety of tasks.
we introduce a framework to learn predictive models that can be triaged to human experts.
we show that predictive models can benefit from algorithmic decision triage, and we provide a gradient-based method to automatically find the best models and triage policy for a given task.
The main takeaway from our work is that
algorithmic triage should be viewed as a differentiable component in the learning process.
the performance of models and human experts under algorithmical triage is interrelated and should be considered simultaneously.
the optimal triaged model is not the same as the model trained for full automation.
